## Overview

The E'ñepa, also called the Panare, are an Indigenous group living in the Amazonian region of Venezuela. Their heartland is in the Guayana Highlands, and their main area is south of Caicara del Orinoco and south of the Orinoco River, in Bolívar State. The Panare number approximately 3,000–4,000 people. They speak Panare, a Cariban language. Their settlements are semi-permanent and generally contain 20 to 80 people. Traditionally hunters and swidden agriculturalists, they have increasingly supplemented their food supply through fishing and livestock raising. Handicrafts provide income for some communities, while wage labour is increasing. Their material culture is changing rapidly.

## Material culture

### Architecture

E'ñepa settlements contain one to four longhouses. These semi-permanent houses are made with thatch from palm leaves. The thatch lasts up to five years before breaking down, after which new houses are constructed, typically in a new location. Settlements host between 20 and 80 people.

## Music & performance

The first episode of the ITV anthropological television series *Disappearing World*, in 1970, focused on the Panare people.

## Festivals & rituals

They state that food is shared within settlement groups and that hearth groups consist of one man, his wife or wives, and their children.

## Foodways

The E'ñepa have traditionally been hunters and swidden agriculturalists. Many have also turned to fishing and livestock raising to augment their food supply. Food is shared within settlement groups, while hearth groups have their own cooking fires. Cooking is done over open fires, and most food is prepared by boiling. Men exclusively conduct fishing and hunting activities, while women typically do most of the cooking; both men and women manage the gardens.

## Language & religion

Panare, also called Eʼñapa Woromaipu, is a Cariban language spoken by the E'ñepa. The autonym *e'ñapá* has several senses depending on context, including “people,” “indigenous-people,” and “Panare-people.” The term “Panare” is described as a Tupí word meaning “friend.” Panare has several subdialects and is spoken west of the Cuchivero basin of the Orinoco River. Its classification within the Cariban family is disputed: one classification places it in the Southern Amazonian branch, while another places it in the Venezuelan Carib branch and the Pemóng-Panare branch. Increasing interaction with Venezuelans has led to widespread bilingualism with Spanish.
